chunks.text: 18-year-old female, Student, resident of Jurong West, Singapore.
Previous pre-op ECG for elective cholecystectomy (age 16, normal results)
General Anesthesia with Spinal Anesthesia (Combined Technique)

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good morning! I'm going to be your anesthesiologist for your laparoscopic appendectomy today. I'd like to go through a few questions to make sure we're all set for your surgery. Can you start by telling me a bit about your current condition and why you're having this surgery?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Morning, doc. I've been having this sharp pain on the right side of my belly for a few days. It started after I ate some street food, I think. The doctor said my appendix is inflamed and needs to come out. So here I am, lah.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for that. Let's move on to your medications. I see here that you're on Montelukast Sodium and Escitalopram. Can you confirm the current doses for me, and let me know if there have been any changes recently?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, I'm still on Montelukast Sodium 10 mg every night for my asthma. But for the Escitalopram, I had it reduced to 5 mg once daily about three months ago. My psychiatrist said it was enough for me, so I've been on that dose since.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for clarifying that. It's important we have the most up-to-date information. Do you have any allergies that we should be aware of?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin. I got a rash the last time I took it, so they told me to avoid it.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Understood. We'll make sure to note that. Now, about your health history — you mentioned asthma. Can you tell me more about that?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: It's pretty mild, doc. I only get it when I exercise really hard or when the weather changes. I use my inhaler maybe once a week, sometimes less. I haven't had any attacks recently.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good to know. And I see you have a BMI of 28, which puts you in the overweight category. Has your weight been stable, or has it been increasing?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: It's been going up a bit, slowly. I try to exercise, but it's hard with my schedule. I know I should lose some weight, but it's tough, you know?

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: It can be challenging, but we'll take that into account during anesthesia. Have you had any previous surgeries or anesthesia? If so, how did you tolerate them?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, this is my first time. I've never been under general anesthesia before, so I'm a bit nervous about that.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That's completely normal. We'll make sure you're comfortable and explain everything as we go. Are you NPO — that is, have you had anything to eat or drink since midnight?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, I stopped eating and drinking after midnight, like the nurse told me. Just a bit thirsty, but I'm okay.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great, thank you. Finally, how are you functioning day-to-day? Can you walk up stairs, carry groceries, that sort of thing?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I can walk and do normal things, but sometimes I get a bit short of breath if I walk too fast or climb too many stairs. But I'm still independent, lah.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for all that information. We'll be using a combined technique — general anesthesia with spinal anesthesia — to make sure you're comfortable during and after the surgery. We'll also monitor you closely given your asthma and weight. Any questions for me before we proceed?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I think that's all. Thanks for explaining everything, doc.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:00] induction propofol one hundred twenty milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:02] fentanyl twenty micrograms

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:05] rocuronium fifty milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:07] tube in, grade one view

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:10] spinal needle inserted, bupivacaine two point five milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:15] lactated ringers one liter given

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:30] mean arterial pressure dropped to fifty five, atenotar one microgram bolus

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:40] desflurane at one point two percent

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:50] surgical incision

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [09:10] normal saline two hundred milliliters bolus

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Hi there, how are you feeling now after the surgery?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I'm okay, I think. A bit sleepy still, but not too bad.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good to hear. Can you tell me your pain level on a scale from 0 to 10, where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst pain?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Maybe around 3 or 4? It's more like a dull ache, not sharp.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Alright, we can manage that with medication. Are you feeling any nausea or did you have any vomiting after waking up?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I haven't vomited, but I feel a bit queasy. Like my stomach is upset.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Understood. We'll keep an eye on that and give you something to help if needed. How's your breathing? Any shortness of breath or wheezing?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I'm breathing fine. Just a bit tired from the anesthesia, I guess.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good. Since you have mild asthma, we want to make sure there's no reaction. Do you remember anything from the operating room or waking up?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Not really. I remember going to sleep and then waking up here. It's all a bit fuzzy.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That's normal with general anesthesia. We also gave you a spinal, so your lower body might feel a bit heavy still. Any concerns or questions for me?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I think that's all. Just want to go home soon.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: We'll get you ready for that soon. Rest well and let the nurses know if you need anything.

18-year-old female undergoing elective laparoscopic appendectomy under general anesthesia with spinal anesthesia (combined technique).

Patient has a history of mild asthma with occasional shortness of breath, is overweight (BMI 28), and is taking Montelukast Sodium for asthma and Escitalopram for anxiety. She is NPO since midnight and has no previous surgical or anesthesia history.

Intraoperative course included administration of Propofol, Fentanyl, Rocuronium, and Bupivacaine via spinal needle. Endotracheal tube placed with Grade 1 view. Mean Arterial Pressure dropped to 55 mmHg, managed with Normal Saline bolus. Desflurane administered for maintenance.

Anticipated issues include risk of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV), airway reactivity or bronchospasm due to asthma history, potential glycemic control issues, increased postoperative pain due to obesity and spinal anesthesia, hemodynamic instability, and a theoretical risk of Serotonin Syndrome.

Monitor for PONV, airway reactivity, blood glucose levels, pain, and hemodynamic stability. Be aware of the potential for serotonin syndrome, though rare. Ensure adequate analgesia and respiratory support as needed.
Patient reports a pain level of 3-4 on a scale of 0-10, described as a dull ache.
Patient experiences nausea (queasiness) but no vomiting post-operatively.
Patient denies shortness of breath or wheezing post-operatively.
Patient has no recall of the operating room or waking up, which is normal with general anesthesia.
Patient's lower body may feel heavy due to spinal anesthesia, as explained by the provider.
Patient is alert and oriented, able to communicate effectively post-operatively.
Patient is eager to go home, indicating a stable and satisfactory recovery thus far.
